The process begins by ingesting the source document, typically a PDF, into a structural parser.
We will utilize GROBID, a machine learning library specifically designed for scholarly articles, to deconstruct the document into a structured format.
This initial step is critical as it identifies and tags the constituent parts of the paper, such as the abstract, introduction, methods, and results sections.

The output is the document's text enriched with sectional metadata, which is vital for later stages, as grammatical and stylistic conventions (e.g., tense usage) vary significantly across these sections.
The core of both models is the self-attention mechanism, which enables the network to compute contextual relationships across the entire sentence.
This is especially useful for scientific text where long-range dependencies frequently occur (e.g., subjects separated from verbs by complex noun phrases).

Using scaled dot-product attention, each token representation is updated by weighting its relevance with respect to all other tokens, while multi-head attention enables simultaneous extraction of syntactic and semantic features.
This ensures that corrections respect both domain terminology and sentence structure.
For complex grammatical rewriting, the system employs a transformer-based encoder-decoder model such as CoEdIT.
The model treats error correction as a conditional text generation task, producing corrected output token-by-token using learned linguistic patterns.
[?] Instruction tuning allows control over the style of edits such as grammatical fixing or formal language enhancement which is crucial for maintaining the scientific tone.
Relative positional embeddings further improve the model's ability to handle long sentences commonly found in academic manuscripts.
For faster, high-confidence adjustments, the system utilizes GECToR, an encoder-only architecture that predicts token-level edit tags instead of regenerating the entire sentence.
These tags (e.g., KEEP, DELETE, REPLACE) enable minimal, targeted corrections without risking loss of meaning.
The model iteratively refines its output, ensuring consistency across dependent grammatical fixes.
Due to linear inference complexity, this component runs efficiently in real-time environments such as Google Colab.

The final output is produced by intelligently combining the strengths of both models generative corrections from CoEdIT for complex grammatical restructuring and fast tagging-based modifications from GECToR for local edits.
This hybrid strategy balances accuracy and computational efficiency while maintaining the author's original scientific intent.
Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) in scientific domains is very different from general grammar correction.
Scientific and engineering papers contain many technical terms, detailed sentence structures, and elements like equations or LaTeX commands that are not part of normal language.
Scientific and engineering manuscripts exhibit a much higher concentration of domain-specific terminology, complex syntactic structures, and non-natural language tokens.
These include mathematical equations, chemical expressions, algorithmic pseudo-code, figure/table references, and structured citation formats (e.g., IEEE, ACM).
Such constructs carry high semantic load and must be preserved verbatim.
Any unintended modification risks altering experimental claims, mathematical correctness, or reproducibility.

General-purpose GEC models, typically trained on learner corpora or web text, optimize for fluency gains and penalize scientific writing characteristics such as passive voice, nominalizations, and discontinuous noun phrases.
These stylistic patterns, however, are core to scientific discourse and reflect pragmatic choices for objectivity and precision.
Consequently, generic models frequently introduce semantic drift, where well-formed scientific content is simplified or restructured in ways that compromise informational fidelity.
Examples include replacing technical jargon with vague synonyms or reordering clauses in a manner that changes causal or temporal relationships.
A further domain-specific obstacle arises from LaTeX markup, which functions as a contextsensitive typesetting language.
LaTeX commands commonly involve hierarchical nesting governed by grammar rules beyond the capability of traditional regular-expression tokenizers.

Neural tokenizers may fragment commands such as \frac{a}{b} into unrelated sub-tokens (, frac, {a}, /, {b}), leading to catastrophic "correction" behaviors including token deletion, brace mismatch, or operator substitution.
Such errors not only degrade semantic accuracy but also generate compilation failures, making the manuscript unusable.
[?] To address these constraints, scientific GEC requires a pipeline architecture that integrates linguistic conservatism with domain-aware structural protection.

The system proposed in this work introduces a dedicated LaTeX masking module that identifies mathematical environments (inline and display modes) using recursive pattern matching and replaces them with immutable placeholders during correction.
This ensures 100% preservation of mathematical content throughout the inference lifecycle.
The correction stage employs a hybrid neural strategy.

A minimal-edit sequence-labeling model (e.g., GECToR) performs deterministic local transformations to handle core grammatical violations (article usage, morphology, agreement) while remaining highly conservative toward sentence structure.
In parallel, a large instruction-tuned generative model (e.g., CoEdIT) is engaged only for clauses containing complex error patterns requiring structural rephrasing.
A weighted filtering mechanism governs its influence to prevent overcorrection.
[?] Finally, a semantic reranking module utilizing SciBERT-based perplexity scoring and cosine similarity to scientific embeddings evaluates multiple candidate outputs.
This component determines whether modifications introduce lexical deviation or meaning shift beyond threshold tolerance.
Candidate sentences with strong semantic alignment to the source and syntactic normalization are selected as final outputs.

[?] Through this integrated workflow LaTeX-aware masking, hybrid constrained correction, and semantic validation, the system maintains a balance between linguistic enhancement and scientific integrity.
The resulting corrections improve readability, coherence, and grammaticality without compromising the mathematical technical precision critical in engineering manuscripts.
The motivation behind this project arises from the increasing demand for a domain-specific grammar correction system tailored to scientific and engineering manuscripts.
In research communication, every detail whether a technical term, mathematical expression, or specific sentence structure carries precise meaning.
Even minor grammatical errors or unclear phrasing can lead to misinterpretation of experimental results and negatively impact the credibility of the work.
Moreover, many scientific papers undergo rigorous editorial and peer-review processes, where clarity, correctness, and consistency in language are essential for successful publication.
However, existing AI-based writing assistants are primarily designed for general-purpose text improvement.
These tools often focus on making sentences sound more fluent or "natural," which can unintentionally modify the author's intended technical meaning.
They also struggle to correctly handle specialized content such as LaTeX equations, algorithmic pseudo-code, and field-specific terminology.
When such elements are mistakenly changed or removed, the document may become scientifically inaccurate or fail to compile entirely.
These limitations highlight the need for a grammar correction system that prioritizes accuracy over aggressive rewriting.
The intended tool should correct grammatical issues, punctuation errors, and stylistic inconsistencies while preserving the author's original scientific content and writing style.
A core objective is to avoid semantic drift and ensure that meaningful scientific details remain unchanged.
This project is motivated by the broader goal of supporting researchers, students, and technical professionals in producing well-structured and publication-ready scientific documents.

By delivering corrections that maintain mathematical fidelity and technical integrity, the sys-tem enables authors to focus on their research outcomes rather than struggling with linguistic challenges.

This complete literature review provides a comprehensive comparative analysis of twenty-four academic writing and grammar-assistance tools, that detail their origins, underlying technologies, functional capabilities, limitations and faults.
These tools include widely recognized platforms such as Grammarly, ProWritingAid, QuillBot, Ginger, and LanguageTool, along with academic-focused tools like Trinka, Paperpal, Writefull, and SciSpace.
Together, they illustrate the current technological landscape of writing support systems used by students, researchers, and professional writers.

The tools differ largely in their technical foundations as some rely on large language models and transformer-based architectures, while others use hybrid approaches that combine rule-based and machine-learning components, and a few operate almost entirely through classical rule-based NLP.
This diversity reflects an evolving field that is shifting from deterministic grammar checking to more context-aware and semantically sensitive AI-driven writing enhancement.
[?] Scientific and engineering texts present unique challenges for grammatical error correction (GEC).

Unlike general writing, these documents contain dense terminology, long syntactic structures, and non-natural language tokens such as equations, pseudo-code, algorithm descriptions, and citation formats.
[?] Across all tools researched, a broad range of error types is detected, including grammar, punctuation, spelling, readability, clarity, style, tone, and wordiness.
Many also offer advanced academic functions such as formal tone preservation, scholarly phrasing suggestions, vocabulary enhancement, and real-time structural feedback.

Some platforms provide domain-specific features tailored to academic writing, such as scientific terminology refinement, journal-style consistency checks, integration with LaTeX workflows, or access to discipline-specific corpora, such as published research articles.
However, despite these strengths, most tools consistently struggle with the complexities of scientific and technical writing.
They often misinterpret domain-specific vocabulary, mishandle mathematical expressions and citations, or fail to maintain semantic coherence in longer research paragraphs.
Several tools also cause issues such as over-correction, where technical precision is often not given priority or provide suggestions that dilute academic tone or alter meaning.
Premium features are frequently paywalled, and transparency regarding model decisions remains limited across many platforms.
This review identifies substantial research gaps that existing tools have not addressed appropriately.

A major gap is the lack of domain-aware editing tailored to STEM disciplines; most tools are not trained on scientific corpora, and therefore perform poorly on specialized terminology and context-heavy academic sentences.
Another issue is inadequate handling of long-form scholarly writing, where tools fail to preserve logical flow, argumentation, and paragraph-level coherence.
Tools also struggle with citation-intensive writing, often breaking references or misinterpreting structured academic syntax.

Additionally, almost all tools lack transparency and explainability, making it difficult for users, especially academic writers, to understand why specific suggestions are made or how corrections affect meaning.
Collectively, these limitations suggest that while many writing assistance systems exist, none fully meet the rigorous demands of scientific manuscript preparation.
[?] Overall, this highlights a clear opportunity for creating a new, domain-specific grammar correction and academic writing enhancement system.

A tool that would integrate scientific terminology awareness, maintain technical precision, support long-form reasoning structures, handle citations and mathematical expressions robustly, and provide transparent, well-justified suggestions.

The documented gaps strongly reinforce the motivation behind developing a specialized academic grammar correction project capable of addressing weaknesses that current commercial and research tools have not resolved.
Commercial grammar tools such as Grammarly, ProWritingAid, QuillBot, Trinka AI, and Paperpal dominate the market.
They offer useful features for readability and clarity, yet none provide a minimal-edit approach tailored for scientific writing.
Most tools are generative, risking authorship concerns and potential AI detection by academic publishers.
Three consistent findings emerge from the literature:
Generative tools excel at paraphrasing, but this presents risks for researchers.
They may unintentionally trigger plagiarism detectors, rewrite technical concepts, or change authorial voice.
These issues are widely documented in academic discussions of AI writing tools.
No reviewed tool prioritizes grammatical correction without rewriting.

Chapter 5
Scientific and engineering documents frequently contain complex grammatical structures, domainspecific terminology, and mathematical expressions written in LaTeX.
Existing grammar correction systems often improve linguistic fluency but fail to preserve the integrity of embedded equations and symbolic notation.
Even minor corruption of mathematical expressions, such
as altering E = mc 2 to textual form, renders the output unusable for academic and scientific purposes.
Additionally, traditional correction approaches rely on single-model architectures that attempt to rewrite entire sentences.
These models are computationally expensive, prone to hallucinations, and unable to efficiently handle large documents containing section-specific writing styles and long-range dependencies.
There is therefore a need for a methodology that:
• Corrects grammatical and stylistic issues in scientific writing while
• Fully preserving LaTeX expressions and mathematical content, and
• Scales efficiently across long technical documents without altering meaning.

The problem addressed in this work is the design of a hybrid correction pipeline that combines recursive masking and tokenization to protect LaTeX regions, a dual-model architecture (Sequence-to-Sequence rewriting and Sequence Tagging) to perform high-quality correction, semantic reranking to prevent hallucination, and post-edit reconstruction to ensure exact restoration of mathematical notation.

The objective is to produce a correction system that improves grammatical accuracy and clarity without modifying the scientific intent, formatting, or mathematical equations present in the original text.

div.head: Preserve Scientific Meaning Through Semantic Verification

p.s: Any modification that alters scientific claims could misrepresent results or lead to misinformation.
To prevent this, the system implements:
• BERTScore-based semantic similarity evaluation
• Pseudo-perplexity scoring to detect unnatural, incoherent rewrites Corrections are only accepted if they remain faithful to the author's intended meaning.
If semantic shifts are detected, the system either falls back to safer corrections or keeps the original text unchanged.

div.head: Maintain the Integrity of LaTeX Structures and Research Formatting

p.s: Research manuscripts include mathematical expressions, references, section labels, fig-
ures, and tables.
Such components must remain untouched.
Therefore, the system:
• Extracts and masks LaTeX environments during processing
• Restores them accurately afterward

div.head: • Ensures zero loss of formatting or equation correctness

p.s: This allows text-only processing while safeguarding critical academic elements.

By incorporating structured metadata (e.g., through GROBID), the system applies corrections that maintain these discipline-specific writing rules, resulting in improved consistency and professionalism.
The system aims to build trust among researchers by focusing on correction accuracy instead of aggression.
Therefore:
• Only unambiguous grammatical errors are corrected
• Stylistic rewriting and paraphrasing are limited
• Authorial tone and sentence structure are respected This approach avoids "over-editing" and reinforces academic integrity standards.

A GEC system that corrects "the data is" to "the data are" but corrupts E = mc 2 to E equals mc squared is functionally useless.
We introduce a robust architecture for LaTeX preservation centered on a "Mask-Correct-Unmask" paradigm.

Neural correction models may generate multiple plausible rewrites.
However, the key constraint of scientific editing is that the meaning must remain unchanged.
To enforce this, we integrate a semantic fidelity module that filters and ranks candidates.
Both GECToR and CoEdIT produce candidate corrections.
These are then evaluated relative to the original sentence.
We compute pairwise semantic similarity scores using Sentence-BERT embeddings.
Candidates exhibiting strong semantic alignment are prioritized, while those deviating from the original meaning are penalized.
If a candidate falls below a similarity threshold, it is discarded outright.
The system then defaults to a more conservative correction (typically GECToR), ensuring that:
• no factual content is altered,
• no claims or numerical values are modified,
• no scientific statements are softened or strengthened unintentionally.

This section presents the preliminary results and functional analysis of our grammar correction tool.
The findings are organized sequentially, corresponding to the distinct stages of our proposed data processing pipeline.
These results serve as a proof-of-concept, demonstrating the successful implementation of the foundational components and validating the overall architectural design.
The aim is to create a comprehensive, reliable, and integrity-conscious writing assistant.
Evaluating grammar correction systems for scientific text is challenging because standard metrics do not reflect scientific correctness.
We therefore combine quantitative metrics with a domain-specific measure of LaTeX preservation.
To evaluate the grammar correction pipeline, a synthetic, domain-specific dataset was created to simulate academic and scientific writing errors.
The dataset was designed to cover a wide variety of edge cases, including:
We report two metrics commonly used in grammatical error correction (GEC):
• GLEU (Generalized LEU): Measures n-gram overlap between the system output and reference corrections.
It correlates better with human judgment than BLEU for editing tasks.
• ERRANT (Error Annotation Toolkit): Classifies edits made by the model, allowing us to inspect whether it mainly fixes punctuation and agreement (desired) or modifies nouns and verbs (undesirable).
These metrics provide a quantitative view of model behavior on scientific writing.

p.s: To ensure that mathematical expressions remain unchanged, we introduce a domain-specific metric, the LaTeX Integrity Score:

div.formula: S latex = N i=1 I(Unmasked i == Original i ) N

A score of S latex = 1.0 indicates that every LaTeX segment was perfectly preserved.
Any value below 1.0 signals a failure in the preservation pipeline.

Once identified, LaTeX segments must be hidden from the GEC model.
We replace the identified segment with a placeholder.
The choice of placeholder is mathematically significant regarding the model's embedding space.
If the mask token belongs to the model's vocabulary, the embedding layer may inject contextual bias.
This can distort nearby corrections or even modify the LaTeX itself.
To combat this, we hash each masked segment at inference time using a cryptographic hash such as SHA-256.
Because each placeholder is unique and out-of-vocabulary, the model treats it as an inert token, eliminating semantic drift.
After correction, hashes are replaced by their corresponding original LaTeX segments from a stored lookup table.
This ensures full restoration without corruption or hallucinated modifications.
